market_context: United States; understanding imported/EU-regulated olive-oil labels
title: What does “cold extracted” mean on olive oil?

seo.title: What does “cold extracted” mean on olive oil?
seo.meta_description: Under EU labeling rules, cold extraction means virgin or extra-virgin olive oil separated by percolation or centrifugation below 27°C (80.6°F). It is a process claim, not a guarantee of superior flavor.
seo.search_intent: Explain the regulated meaning of cold extraction on olive-oil labels, the 27°C threshold and how it differs from first cold pressing.

excerpt: On EU-regulated olive-oil labels, “cold extraction” has a specific meaning: virgin or extra-virgin olive oil obtained by percolation or centrifugation of olive paste below 27°C (80.6°F). It does not mean the olives were never warmed, and it does not by itself guarantee better flavor. It describes extraction temperature and method.
content_html:
“Cold extracted” sounds like a loose marketing phrase, but on olive oils sold under EU labeling rules it has a precise definition. The key threshold is 27°C (80.6°F), and the separation method is percolation or centrifugation.

What the regulated claim means

EU Delegated Regulation 2022/2104 allows the term cold extraction only for virgin or extra-virgin olive oils obtained below 27°C by percolation or centrifugation of the olive paste.

It is therefore not a generic phrase that can be placed freely on any refined olive-oil product.

What happens before the oil is separated

Olives are milled into a paste. That paste is slowly mixed during malaxation so tiny oil droplets combine and become easier to separate.

Temperature affects the balance between extraction yield and preservation of aroma compounds. Warmer conditions can make separation easier, while more moderate temperatures can help limit losses of some volatile compounds.

Cold does not mean no heat at all

The paste can be warmer than the surrounding room and still meet the claim as long as the regulated extraction condition remains below 27°C. Cold extraction is a legal threshold, not a promise that the process happens at refrigerator temperature.

It is not the same as first cold pressed

EU rules reserve first cold pressing for virgin or extra-virgin oils obtained below 27°C by a first mechanical pressing using traditional hydraulic presses.

Most modern mills use centrifugation, so cold extraction is the more relevant term for contemporary production.

Does cold extraction guarantee better oil?

No. Extra-virgin status still requires chemical compliance and sensory quality without defects. Cultivar, fruit maturity, olive condition, processing speed, oxygen exposure and storage all affect the finished oil.

How to read the label

Treat the phrase as useful process information: the oil was mechanically separated from olive paste below 27°C using the specified methods. It does not replace freshness, sensory quality or the extra-virgin category itself.

faq.question: What temperature counts as cold extraction?
faq.answer: Under EU rules, below 27°C (80.6°F) for virgin or extra-virgin oil obtained by percolation or centrifugation.

faq.question: Does cold extracted mean no heat was used?
faq.answer: No. It means the regulated extraction condition stayed below the 27°C threshold.

faq.question: Is cold extracted the same as first cold pressed?
faq.answer: No. First cold pressing refers to a traditional first mechanical pressing below 27°C using hydraulic presses; cold extraction refers to percolation or centrifugation.
